citation.title: Randomization-based confidence sets for the local average treatment effect

standing_assumptions: [Units, potential outcomes, compliance: main p. 3 (PDF p. 3), Section 2.1] We consider an experiment with $n$ units, where each unit is randomized to treatment or control. Let $y_i(d, z)$ denote the potential outcome of unit $i$ under the potential compliance decision $d \in \{0, 1\}$ and the treatment assignment $z \in \{0, 1\}$. Let $d_i(z)$ denote the compliance decision of the $i$th unit when under treatment status $z$. We write $d_i(1) = 0$ if the $i$th unit is assigned to treatment, but does not receive treatment, and write $d_i(1) = 1$ if it does. The compliance decision $d_i(0)$ under assignment to control is defined analogously. [...] Let $[n] = \{1, \ldots, n\}$. Assumption 1 (Exclusion restriction). For all $i \in [n]$, $y_i(d, z)$ is independent of $z$. This assumption implies that treatment assignment affects outcomes only through treatment receipt, and hence $y_i(d, 1) = y_i(d, 0)$ for all $i \in [n]$. Given this assumption, we write $y_i(d)$ from now on to denote the potential outcome under treatment status $d$. [main p. 4 (PDF p. 4)] Assumption 2 (Monotonicity). For all $i \in [n]$, we have $d_i(1) \ge d_i(0)$. Let $\mathcal{C}$ denote the set of compliers, $\mathcal{C} = \{i \in [n] : d_i(0) = 0,\ d_i(1) = 1\}$. (1) Our inferential target is the LATE in the experimental sample, defined by $\bar\beta = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}|}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{C}}\{y_i(1) - y_i(0)\}$. (2) We assume throughout the paper that there is at least one complier ($|\mathcal{C}| \ge 1$) so that the quantity is well-defined. [Design and data: main p. 4, Section 2.2] We assume that the experiments under consideration are completely randomized: among $n$ units, researchers assign $n_1$ units to treatment, chosen uniformly at random. [...] For each unit $i$, we let $Z_i$ be a random variable such that $Z_i = 1$ if unit $i$ is assigned to treatment and $Z_i = 0$ otherwise. By definition, $\mathrm{pr}(Z_i = 1) = n_1/n$, and we introduce the shorthand $\pi = n_1/n$. For each unit $i$, researchers observe compliance decisions $D_i = d_i(Z_i)$ and outcomes $Y_i = y_i(D_i)$. Each unit $i$ may additionally be associated with some covariate information [...]; if so, this information is collected in a column vector $x_i \in \mathbb{R}^k$. Throughout the paper we assume that $k$ does not change with the sample size $n$. [...] We adopt the finite-population (design-based) framework, treating the potential outcomes and compliance decisions as fixed parameters [...]. The sole source of randomness in our model is the vector of random treatment assignments, and statistical uncertainties are evaluated exclusively with respect to this randomness. [Studentized statistic: main pp. 4-5, Section 3.1] For all $\beta \in \mathbb{R}$, we define the statistic $\hat\tau(\beta) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \beta D_i)(Z_i - \pi)$. [...] A short calculation shows that $\hat\tau(\beta) = \pi(1-\pi)\left\{\frac{1}{n_1}\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i(Y_i - \beta D_i) - \frac{1}{n_0}\sum_{i=1}^n (1 - Z_i)(Y_i - \beta D_i)\right\}$, where $n_0 = n - n_1$ [...]. We further define $\hat v_i(1, \beta) = Y_i - \beta D_i - \frac{1}{n_1}\sum_{j=1}^n Z_j(Y_j - \beta D_j)$, $\hat v_i(0, \beta) = Y_i - \beta D_i - \frac{1}{n_0}\sum_{j=1}^n (1 - Z_j)(Y_j - \beta D_j)$. (3) Using this notation, we define the variance estimator $\hat\sigma^2(\beta) = \frac{\pi^2(1-\pi)^2}{n_1^2}\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i\hat v_i^2(1, \beta) + \frac{\pi^2(1-\pi)^2}{n_0^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (1 - Z_i)\hat v_i^2(0, \beta)$ and the studentized statistic $\Delta(\beta) = \frac{\hat\tau(\beta)}{\hat\sigma(\beta)}$. (4) We will use the absolute value $|\Delta(\beta)|$ as our test statistic and construct confidence sets by test inversion. We refer to the test statistic $\Delta(\beta)$ in (4) as the AR statistic. [Randomization distribution and confidence set: main pp. 5-6, Section 3.2] The assignment vector $Z = (Z_1, \ldots, Z_n)$ is a random vector in $\{0, 1\}^n$. Let $Z^*$ be a random vector with the same distribution as $Z$ and which is independent of $Z$. We use $\mathbb{P}^*$ to denote the conditional (on $Z$) probability measure induced by $Z^*$. We define $\hat\tau^* : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ by $\hat\tau^*(\beta) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \beta D_i)(Z_i^* - \pi)$, where we recall that by definition $Y_i$ and $D_i$ depend only on $Z_i$ and not on $Z_i^*$. We also define the variance estimator $\hat\sigma^{*2}(\beta) = \frac{\pi^2(1-\pi)^2}{n_1^2}\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i^*\left\{Y_i - \beta D_i - \frac{1}{n_1}\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i^*(Y_i - \beta D_i)\right\}^2 + \frac{\pi^2(1-\pi)^2}{n_0^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (1 - Z_i^*)\left\{Y_i - \beta D_i - \frac{1}{n_0}\sum_{i=1}^n (1 - Z_i^*)(Y_i - \beta D_i)\right\}^2$ [the inner sums are the reassigned-arm means; the paper reuses the index $i$] and the studentized statistic $\Delta^*(\beta) = \frac{\hat\tau^*(\beta)}{\hat\sigma^*(\beta)}$. (5) The distribution of $|\Delta^*(\beta)|$ under $\mathbb{P}^*$ is discrete and supported on $[0, \infty]$. For every $\alpha \in (0, 1)$, there exists a smallest (possibly infinite) value $\eta^*_{1-\alpha}(\beta, Z)$ such that $\mathbb{P}^*\{|\Delta^*(\beta)| \le \eta^*_{1-\alpha}(\beta, Z)\} \ge 1 - \alpha$. (6) Our confidence set is defined as $I^*_{1-\alpha}(Z) = \{\beta \in \mathbb{R} : |\Delta(\beta)| \le \eta^*_{1-\alpha}(\beta, Z)\}$. (7) [Assumptions 3 and 4, parameter space $\Theta_n$: main pp. 6-8] Assumption 3 (Parameter space). Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and constants $\delta < 1$ and $A > 0$ be given. Set $w_i(1) = y_i\{d_i(1)\} - \bar\beta d_i(1)$, $w_i(0) = y_i\{d_i(0)\} - \bar\beta d_i(0)$. The following conditions on the potential outcomes and compliance decisions hold. (i) For the given $\delta$, $\sigma_{w(1),w(0),\mathcal{C}} \ge -\delta\,\sigma_{w(1),\mathcal{C}}\,\sigma_{w(0),\mathcal{C}}$. Here, $\sigma_{w(1),w(0),\mathcal{C}}$ is the complier-group covariance of adjusted potential outcomes, $\sigma_{w(1),w(0),\mathcal{C}} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}| - 1}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{C}}\{w_i(1) - \mu_{w(1),\mathcal{C}}\}\{w_i(0) - \mu_{w(0),\mathcal{C}}\}$, where $\mu_{w(a),\mathcal{C}} = |\mathcal{C}|^{-1}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{C}} w_i(a)$ for $a \in \{0, 1\}$, and $\sigma^2_{w(1),\mathcal{C}}$ and $\sigma^2_{w(0),\mathcal{C}}$ are the complier-group potential outcome variances, $\sigma^2_{w(a),\mathcal{C}} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}| - 1}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{C}}\{w_i(a) - \mu_{w(a),\mathcal{C}}\}^2$ for $a \in \{0, 1\}$. If $|\mathcal{C}| = 1$, all variances and covariances are defined to be zero. (ii) For each $a \in \{0, 1\}$ and the given $A$, $\left\{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n |w_i(a) - \mu_{w(a)}|^4\right\}^{1/4} \le A\sigma_{w(a)}$, where $\mu_{w(a)} = n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n w_i(a)$ and $\sigma^2_{w(a)} = (n-1)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n \{w_i(a) - \mu_{w(a)}\}^2$. [...] Assumption 4 (Completely randomized experiment). Given $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and a constant $0 < r \le 1/2$, we have $n_1 \in [rn, (1-r)n]$. We denote the parameter space of potential outcomes, compliance decisions and experimental designs satisfying Assumptions 1-4 with $n$ units and constants $\delta$, $r$ and $A$ by $\Theta_n(\delta, r, A) = \left\{\left(\{(y_i(1), y_i(0), d_i(1), d_i(0))\}_{i=1}^n, \Pi_n\right)\right\}$, where $\{(y_i(1), y_i(0), d_i(1), d_i(0))\}_{i=1}^n$ satisfies Assumption 3 with constants $\delta$ and $A$, and $\Pi_n$ is a distribution of random assignment variables $\{Z_i\}_{i=1}^n$ implementing complete randomization that satisfies Assumption 4 with constant $r$. Each combination of potential outcomes, compliance decisions and an experimental design completely determines the distribution of our test statistic. [...] For each parameter $\theta$ in the parameter space, we denote its LATE by $\bar\beta(\theta)$. [Regression adjustment: main pp. 8-10, Sections 4.1-4.3] [...] each unit $i$ comes equipped with a column vector $x_i \in \mathbb{R}^k$ of covariates for some $k \in \mathbb{N}$. We suppose that each $x_i$ is demeaned, meaning that $\sum_{i=1}^n x_i = 0_k$, where $0_k$ denotes the zero vector in $\mathbb{R}^k$. [...] We denote the $s$th element of $x_i$ by $x_{si}$. Given a $\beta \in \mathbb{R}$ and a treatment assignment vector $Z$, consider the linear regression $Y_i - \beta D_i \sim (1 - Z_i)\varphi_0 + Z_i\varphi_1 + (1 - Z_i)x_i'\gamma_0 + Z_i x_i'\gamma_1$. (8) This is an interacted linear regression that regresses $Y_i - \beta D_i$ on $((1 - Z_i), Z_i, (1 - Z_i)x_i, Z_i x_i)$ without an intercept. For each $\beta$, denote the ordinary least squares (OLS) estimators resulting from (8) by $\hat\varphi(0, \beta)$, $\hat\varphi(1, \beta)$, $\hat\gamma(0, \beta)$ and $\hat\gamma(1, \beta)$, corresponding to the order in which the associated coefficients appear in (8). We define the randomization statistics $\hat\varphi^*(0, \beta)$, $\hat\varphi^*(1, \beta)$, $\hat\gamma^*(0, \beta)$ and $\hat\gamma^*(1, \beta)$ similarly by using $Z^*$ instead of $Z$. [main p. 9] We define the covariate-adjusted difference-in-means statistic as $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta) = \frac{1}{n_1}\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i\{Y_i - \beta D_i - x_i'\hat\gamma(1, \beta)\} - \frac{1}{n_0}\sum_{i=1}^n (1 - Z_i)\{Y_i - \beta D_i - x_i'\hat\gamma(0, \beta)\}$, (9) and we define the covariate-adjusted randomization estimator $\hat\tau^*_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)$ analogously, again replacing $Z_i$ by $Z_i^*$ and replacing $\hat\gamma(0, \beta)$ and $\hat\gamma(1, \beta)$ by their randomization analogues. [...] The residual estimators associated with (8) and their randomization-based counterparts are $\hat\varepsilon_i(\beta) = Y_i - \beta D_i - \hat\varphi(Z_i, \beta) - x_i'\hat\gamma(Z_i, \beta)$, $\hat\varepsilon_i^*(\beta) = Y_i - \beta D_i - \hat\varphi^*(Z_i^*, \beta) - x_i'\hat\gamma^*(Z_i^*, \beta)$. We use these to define the variance estimators $\hat\sigma^2_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta) = \frac{1}{n_1^2}\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i\hat\varepsilon_i(\beta)^2 + \frac{1}{n_0^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (1 - Z_i)\hat\varepsilon_i(\beta)^2$, $\hat\sigma^{2*}_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta) = \frac{1}{n_1^2}\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i^*\hat\varepsilon_i^*(\beta)^2 + \frac{1}{n_0^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (1 - Z_i^*)\hat\varepsilon_i^*(\beta)^2$. The adjusted studentized difference-in-means statistics are then $\Delta_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta) = \frac{\hat\tau_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)}{\hat\sigma_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)}$, $\Delta^*_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta) = \frac{\hat\tau^*_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)}{\hat\sigma^*_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)}$. (10) [...] Given $\alpha \in (0, 1)$, there exists a smallest (possibly infinite) value $\eta^{\mathrm{adj},*}_{1-\alpha}(\beta, Z)$ such that $\mathbb{P}^*\{|\Delta^*_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)| \le \eta^{\mathrm{adj},*}_{1-\alpha}(\beta, Z)\} \ge 1 - \alpha$. [main p. 10] Our proposed confidence set is $I^{\mathrm{adj},*}_{1-\alpha}(Z) = \{\beta \in \mathbb{R} : |\Delta_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)| \le \eta^{\mathrm{adj},*}_{1-\alpha}(\beta, Z)\}$. (11) [Assumption 5 and parameter space $\Xi_n$: main pp. 10-11] Assumption 5. Let $k, n \in \mathbb{N}$ and constants $\delta < 1$ and $\tilde\varepsilon, A, B > 0$ be given. For each $a \in \{0, 1\}$, define $\varepsilon_i(a, \bar\beta) = y_i\{d_i(a)\} - \bar\beta d_i(a) - \varphi(a, \bar\beta) - x_i'\gamma(a, \bar\beta)$. The following conditions on the potential outcomes, compliance decisions and covariates hold. (i) For the given $\delta$, $\sigma_{\varepsilon(1,\bar\beta),\varepsilon(0,\bar\beta)} \ge -\delta\sigma_{\varepsilon(1,\bar\beta)}\sigma_{\varepsilon(0,\bar\beta)}$. (ii) For each $a \in \{0, 1\}$ and the given $B$, $\left\{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \varepsilon_i^4(a, \bar\beta)\right\}^{1/4} \le B\sigma_{\varepsilon(a,\bar\beta)}$. (iii) We have that $\sum_{i=1}^n x_i = 0_k$. (iv) For all $s \in [k]$ and the given $A$, we have that $n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n x_{si}^4 \le A$. (v) Let $\lambda_{\min}$ denote the smallest eigenvalue of $n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i x_i'$. Then for the given $\tilde\varepsilon$, $\lambda_{\min} \ge \tilde\varepsilon$. We denote the parameter space of potential outcomes, compliance decisions, covariates and experimental designs satisfying Assumptions 1, 2, 4 and 5 with $n$ units, covariates of dimension $k$, and constants $\delta$, $\tilde\varepsilon$, $A$, $B$ and $r$ by $\Xi_n(k, \delta, \tilde\varepsilon, A, B, r) = \left\{\left(\{(y_i(1), y_i(0), d_i(1), d_i(0), x_i)\}_{i=1}^n, \Pi_n\right)\right\}$. Here, $\{(y_i(1), y_i(0), d_i(1), d_i(0), x_i)\}_{i=1}^n$ satisfies Assumption 5 with constants $\delta$, $\tilde\varepsilon$, $A$ and $B$, and $\Pi_n$ is a distribution of random assignment variables $\{Z_i\}_{i=1}^n$ implementing complete randomization that satisfies Assumption 4 with constant $r$. [The population variances and covariance in Assumption 5 are those of Supplement A.1 below, with divisor $n - 1$; $\varphi(a, \beta)$, $\gamma(a, \beta)$ are defined in Supplement D.2 below.] [Supplement A, notation: Supplement p. 21 (Supplement PDF p. 1)] We let $\mathbb{N}$ denote the positive integers [...]. We use the notation $\lesssim$ to denote inequalities that hold up to a constant independent of $n$. [...] We also define a set $\mathcal{A}$ of always-takers and a set $\mathcal{N}$ of never-takers by $\mathcal{A} = \{i \in [n] : d_i(0) = 1, d_i(1) = 1\}$, $\mathcal{N} = \{i \in [n] : d_i(0) = 0, d_i(1) = 0\}$. Let $\mathcal{T}(1), \mathcal{T}(0) \subset [n]$ denote the sets of subjects in the treatment and control groups defined by $Z$, respectively, so that $\mathcal{T}(1) = \{i \in [n] : Z_i = 1\}$, $\mathcal{T}(0) = \{i \in [n] : Z_i = 0\}$. Given a vector $v$, we use $\|v\|_2$ to denote the standard $l_2$ vector norm. [...] A.1. For any vector $q = (q_i)_{i=1}^n \in \mathbb{R}^n$, we define the population mean and variance by $\mu_q = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n q_i$, $\sigma_q^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (q_i - \mu_q)^2$. We also define within-group variances for each group $G \in \{\mathcal{A}, \mathcal{C}, \mathcal{N}\}$ by $\sigma^2_{q,G} = \frac{1}{|G| - 1}\sum_{i \in G}(q_i - \mu_{q,G})^2$, where $\mu_{q,G} = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{i \in G} q_i$ if $|G| \ge 2$ and zero otherwise. Given an additional vector $\tilde q = (\tilde q_i)_{i=1}^n \in \mathbb{R}^n$, we define the population covariance by $\sigma_{q\tilde q} = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (q_i - \mu_q)(\tilde q_i - \mu_{\tilde q})$, and the within-group covariances by $\sigma_{q\tilde q,G} = \frac{1}{|G| - 1}\sum_{i \in G}(q_i - \mu_{q,G})(\tilde q_i - \mu_{\tilde q,G})$, if $|G| \ge 2$ and zero otherwise. A.2. Let $\mathcal{Z}$ be a mean zero, variance one normal random variable. [...] For an $\alpha \in (0, 1)$, define $z_{1-\alpha} \in \mathbb{R}$ as the value such that $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{Z} > z_{1-\alpha}) = \alpha$. [Supplement B.1 and B.3: Supplement p. 22 (PDF p. 2)] Lemma 2. For all $\beta \in \mathbb{R}$, the variance of $\hat\tau(\beta)$ is $\operatorname{var}(\hat\tau(\beta)) = \frac{S_1^2(\beta)}{n_1} + \frac{S_0^2(\beta)}{n_0} - \frac{S_{10}^2(\beta)}{n}$, (B.1) where $S_1^2(\beta) = \frac{\pi^2(1-\pi)^2}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n v_i(1, \beta)^2$, $S_0^2(\beta) = \frac{\pi^2(1-\pi)^2}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n v_i(0, \beta)^2$, $S_{10}^2(\beta) = \frac{\pi^2(1-\pi)^2}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (v_i(1, \beta) - v_i(0, \beta))^2$, (B.2) $v_i(1, \beta) = y_i(d_i(1)) - \beta d_i(1) - \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i(d_i(1)) - \beta d_i(1))$, (B.3) $v_i(0, \beta) = y_i(d_i(0)) - \beta d_i(0) - \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i(d_i(0)) - \beta d_i(0))$. (B.4) [...] Lemma 3. We have $E[\hat\tau(\beta)] = 0$ when $\beta = |\mathcal{C}|^{-1}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{C}}(y_i(1) - y_i(0))$. [Supplement C, conventions: Supplement p. 23 (PDF p. 3)] Throughout this section, we let $\delta, r, A$ be the constants fixed in the statement of Theorem 1, and set $\Theta_n = \Theta_n(\delta, r, A)$. The notation $\Theta_n$ encodes Assumptions 1-4. We typically denote elements of $\Theta_n$ by $\theta_n$. For each model $\theta_n$, we denote its local average treatment effect by $\bar\beta(\theta_n)$ [...]. In various lemmas below, we will consider subsequences $(\theta_{n_k})_{k=1}^\infty$ of a given sequence $(\theta_n)_{n=1}^\infty$ of models. We let $n_{1k}$ denote the number of elements in the treatment group of $\theta_{n_k}$, and $n_{0k}$ the number of elements in the control group of $\theta_{n_k}$, so that $n_{0k} + n_{1k} = n_k$. [...] For the remainder of the proofs, we will implicitly assume that the variances $\sigma^2_{w(a)}$, for $a \in \{0, 1\}$ as defined in Assumption 3, are both strictly positive. This entails no loss of generality provided we adopt the convention that $0/0 = 0$. If both variances are zero, then the complier treatment effect is constant and additive, so the exact coverage result of the randomization-based CI in Imbens & Rosenbaum (2005) applies. [...] Similar comments apply to the proofs in Section D. [...] In results on sequences $(\theta_n)_{n=1}^\infty$, we will generally omit the $n$-dependence on $w_i(1)$, $w_i(0)$, and other model-dependent quantities for brevity. [Supplement C.3: Supplement pp. 27-28 (PDF pp. 7-8)] We write $E^*$ and $\operatorname{var}^*$ for expectation and variance under the probability measure $\mathbb{P}^*$. By Lemma 3, for any $\beta$ we have $E^*[\hat\tau^*(\beta)] = 0$, and by Lemma 2, $\operatorname{var}^*(\hat\tau^*(\beta)) = \frac{S_1^{*2}(\beta)}{n_1} + \frac{S_0^{*2}(\beta)}{n_0}$, (C.25) where $S_1^{*2}(\beta) = S_0^{*2}(\beta) = \frac{\pi^2(1-\pi)^2}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n \left(Y_i - \beta D_i - \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \beta D_i)\right)^2$. (C.26) [...] We recall that $\mu_Y = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i$, $\mu_D = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n D_i$ and define $\hat\mu_{y(d(a))} = \frac{1}{n_a}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{T}(a)} y_i(d_i(a))$, $\hat\mu_{d(a)} = \frac{1}{n_a}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{T}(a)} d_i(a)$, for each $a \in \{0, 1\}$. [Supplement D, least-squares parameters and infeasible estimator: Supplement pp. 31-32 (PDF pp. 11-12)] We let $k, \delta, \tilde\varepsilon, A, B, r$ be the constants fixed in the statement of Theorem 2, and set $\Xi_n = \Xi_n(k, \delta, \tilde\varepsilon, A, B, r)$. D.2. Suppose a $\beta \in \mathbb{R}$ is given. Then we define, for each $a \in \{0, 1\}$, outcomes $w_i(a, \beta)$ by $w_i(a, \beta) = y_i(d_i(a)) - \beta d_i(a)$. (D.1) We define the least-squares regression parameters $\varphi(a, \beta) : \{0, 1\} \times \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $\gamma(a, \beta) : \{0, 1\} \times \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^k$, by $(\varphi(a, \beta), \gamma(a, \beta)) = \arg\min_{(s,t) \in \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}^k}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (w_i(a, \beta) - s - x_i't)^2$, (D.2) where we interpret $t$ as a column vector. We define the residuals for (D.2) by $\varepsilon_i(a, \beta) = w_i(a, \beta) - \varphi(a, \beta) - x_i'\gamma(a, \beta)$. The parameters $\varphi^*(a, \beta)$ and $\gamma^*(a, \beta)$ are defined similarly, by replacing $w_i(a, \beta)$ with $Y_i - \beta D_i$ in (D.2), and we define the associated residuals $\varepsilon_i^*(\beta)$ by $\varepsilon_i^*(\beta) = Y_i - \beta D_i - \varphi^*(a, \beta) - x_i'\gamma^*(a, \beta)$. (D.3) These definitions imply that $\varphi^*(0, \beta) = \varphi^*(1, \beta)$ and $\gamma^*(0, \beta) = \gamma^*(1, \beta)$. D.3. To analyze the asymptotic behavior of $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)$, we define the infeasible estimator $\tilde\tau_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta) = \frac{1}{n_1}\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i(Y_i - \beta D_i - x_i'\gamma(1, \beta)) - \frac{1}{n_0}\sum_{i=1}^n (1 - Z_i)(Y_i - \beta D_i - x_i'\gamma(0, \beta))$. (D.4) The infeasible estimator $\tilde\tau^*_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)$ is defined similarly, replacing $Z_i$ by $Z_i^*$, and $\gamma(1, \beta)$ and $\gamma(0, \beta)$ by $\gamma^*(1, \beta)$ and $\gamma^*(0, \beta)$, respectively. A straightforward adaptation of Lemma 2 shows that $\operatorname{var}(\tilde\tau_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)) = \frac{\mathcal{S}_1^2(\beta)}{n_1} + \frac{\mathcal{S}_0^2(\beta)}{n_0} - \frac{\mathcal{S}_{10}^2(\beta)}{n}$, (D.5) where $\mathcal{S}_1^2(\beta) = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n \varepsilon_i^2(1, \beta)$, $\mathcal{S}_0^2(\beta) = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n \varepsilon_i^2(0, \beta)$, $\mathcal{S}_{10}^2(\beta) = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (\varepsilon_i(1, \beta) - \varepsilon_i(0, \beta))^2$. Similarly, $\operatorname{var}^*(\tilde\tau^*_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)) = \frac{\mathcal{S}_{1,*}^2(\beta)}{n_1} + \frac{\mathcal{S}_{0,*}^2(\beta)}{n_0}$, $\mathcal{S}_{1,*}^2(\beta) = \mathcal{S}_{0,*}^2(\beta) = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n \varepsilon_i^*(\beta)^2$. (D.6) [Supplement E.1: Supplement p. 32 (PDF p. 12)] Denote $x_i^\circ = [0, x_i']' \in \mathbb{R}^{k+1}$ and $\tilde x_i = [1, x_i']' \in \mathbb{R}^{k+1}$. For $a \in \{0, 1\}$, define $\psi(a, \beta) = \begin{bmatrix}\varphi(a, \beta) \\ \gamma(a, \beta)\end{bmatrix}$, $\hat\psi(a, \beta) = \begin{bmatrix}\hat\varphi(a, \beta) \\ \hat\gamma(a, \beta)\end{bmatrix}$. (E.1) We denote their randomization counterparts as $\psi^*(a, \beta)$ and $\hat\psi^*(a, \beta)$. Lemma 14. The following claims hold. 1. canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statements refuted: main p. 8 (PDF p. 8)] Theorem 1. Fix $\alpha \in (0, 1)$, $\delta < 1$, $r \in (0, 1/2]$ and $A > 0$. Let $\Theta_n(\delta, r, A)$ be the parameter space of models that satisfy Assumptions 1-4 with these constants. Then $\lim_{n\to\infty}\inf_{\beta\in\mathbb{R}}\inf_{\{\theta\in\Theta_n(\delta,r,A):\,\bar\beta(\theta)=\beta\}}\mathbb{P}_\theta\{\beta \in I^*_{1-\alpha}(Z)\} = 1 - \alpha$. Remark 3. The infimum of the coverage rates of the confidence sets is equal to $1 - \alpha$ because some constant-additive-effect models belong to the set $\Theta_n(\delta, r, A)$. In the design-based setting, the variance is not identified, and a conservative variance bound must instead be estimated (Aronow et al., 2014; Imbens & Rubin, 2015). The asymptotic coverage rate is bounded below by $1 - \alpha$ for many data-generating processes, and is exactly $1 - \alpha$ when the data are generated under a constant-additive-effect model. [main p. 11 (PDF p. 11)] Theorem 2. Fix $k \in \mathbb{N}$, $\alpha \in (0, 1)$, $r \in (0, 1/2]$, $\delta < 1$ and $\tilde\varepsilon, A, B > 0$. Let $\Xi_n(k, \delta, \tilde\varepsilon, A, B, r)$ be the parameter space of models that satisfy Assumptions 1, 2, 4 and 5 with these constants. Then $\lim_{n\to\infty}\inf_{\beta\in\mathbb{R}}\inf_{\{\theta\in\Xi_n(k,\delta,\tilde\varepsilon,A,B,r):\,\bar\beta(\theta)=\beta\}}\mathbb{P}_\theta\{\beta \in I^{\mathrm{adj},*}_{1-\alpha}(Z)\} = 1 - \alpha$. [Printed proof step refuted: Supplement p. 31 (PDF p. 11)] Finally, note that a sequence of constant-additive-effect models belongs to our parameter set. Hence the inequality holds as an equality. [Counterexample, from the validators; the convention $0/0 = 0$ of Supplement p. 23 is used.] (a) [Moment collapse.] Let $n \ge 2$ and $v_1, \ldots, v_n \in \mathbb{R}$. If $\left\{\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n v_i^4\right\}^{1/4} \le \frac12\left\{\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n v_i^2\right\}^{1/2}$, then $v_i = 0$ for all $i$. [Because $\left(\sum_i v_i^2\right)^2 \le n\sum_i v_i^4$ and the hypothesis gives $16(n-1)^2\sum_i v_i^4 \le n\left(\sum_i v_i^2\right)^2$, so that $\{16(n-1)^2 - n^2\}\left(\sum_i v_i^2\right)^2 \le 0$, with $16(n-1)^2 - n^2 = 15(n-2)^2 + 28(n-2) + 12 > 0$.] (b) [Theorem 1 fails for $(\delta, r, A) = (0, 1/4, 1/2)$.] Let $n \ge 2$ and let $\theta$ be any model in $\Theta_n(0, 1/4, 1/2)$, with $\beta = \bar\beta(\theta)$. By (a) applied to $v_i = w_i(a) - \mu_{w(a)}$ and Assumption 3(ii) with $A = 1/2$, $w_i(a) = c_a$ for all $i$, for each $a \in \{0, 1\}$; and $c_1 = c_0$, because $n(c_1 - c_0) = \sum_{i=1}^n \{w_i(1) - w_i(0)\} = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{C}}\{y_i(1) - y_i(0) - \beta\} = 0$. Hence for every assignment $Y_i - \beta D_i = c$ for all $i$, $\hat\tau(\beta) = 0$, $\hat\sigma^2(\beta) = 0$ and $\Delta(\beta) = 0/0 = 0$; likewise $\Delta^*(\beta) = 0$ for every $Z^*$, so $\eta^*_{1-\alpha}(\beta, Z) = 0$ and $\beta \in I^*_{1-\alpha}(Z)$. So $\mathbb{P}_\theta\{\beta \in I^*_{1-\alpha}(Z)\} = 1$ for every model in the class. The class is non-empty for every $n \ge 2$ and every $\beta \in \mathbb{R}$: take all units compliers, $d_i(0) = 0$, $d_i(1) = 1$, $y_i(0) = 0$, $y_i(1) = \beta$, and $n_1 = \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ (then $w_i(1) = w_i(0) = 0$, Assumption 3(i) reads $0 \ge 0$, 3(ii) reads $0 \le 0$, and $n/4 \le \lfloor n/2 \rfloor \le 3n/4$). Therefore $\inf_{\beta\in\mathbb{R}}\inf_{\{\theta\in\Theta_n(0,1/4,1/2):\,\bar\beta(\theta)=\beta\}}\mathbb{P}_\theta\{\beta \in I^*_{1-\alpha}(Z)\} = 1$ for every $n \ge 2$ and every $\alpha \in (0, 1)$; the limit is $1 \ne 1 - \alpha$. The models exhibited have constant additive effects, so the last sentence of Remark 3 and the last step of the proof of Theorem 1 fail for this class as well. (c) [Theorem 2 fails for $(k, \delta, \tilde\varepsilon, A, B, r) = (1, 0, 1/4, 4, 1/2, 1/4)$.] Let $n \ge 2$ and let $\theta$ be any model in $\Xi_n(1, 0, 1/4, 4, 1/2, 1/4)$, with $\beta = \bar\beta(\theta)$. The population residuals $\varepsilon_i(a, \beta)$ have mean zero, so by (a) and Assumption 5(ii) with $B = 1/2$, $\varepsilon_i(a, \beta) = 0$ for all $i$ and $a$: $w_i(a, \beta) = \varphi(a, \beta) + \gamma(a, \beta)x_i$, and $\varphi(1, \beta) = \varphi(0, \beta)$. On the event that, in each arm, the observed covariate values are not all equal (so that both arm regressions of (8) have full column rank), the fitted coefficients equal $(\varphi(a, \beta), \gamma(a, \beta))$, all fitted residuals are zero, $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta) = 0$ and $\Delta_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta) = 0 \le \eta^{\mathrm{adj},*}_{1-\alpha}(\beta, Z)$, so $\beta \in I^{\mathrm{adj},*}_{1-\alpha}(Z)$. With $Q = n^{-1}\sum_i x_i^2 \ge 1/4$ and $n^{-1}\sum_i x_i^4 \le 4$, the probability that a given arm (of size $m \in [n/4, 3n/4]$) fails to have full column rank is at most $258\,\frac{n - m}{m(n-1)} \le \frac{774}{n-1}$ (Chebyshev's inequality for the arm means of $x_i$ and $x_i^2$ under simple random sampling), so the probability that either arm fails is at most $1548/(n-1)$, uniformly over the class. Hence $\mathbb{P}_\theta\{\beta \in I^{\mathrm{adj},*}_{1-\alpha}(Z)\} \ge \max\{0, 1 - 1548/(n-1)\}$ for every model in the class, whatever is decided for rank-deficient arms. The class is non-empty for every $n \ge 2$ and every $\beta \in \mathbb{R}$: all units compliers, $y_i(0) = 0$, $y_i(1) = \beta$, $n_1 = \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ and $x_i = (2i - n - 1)/n$, for which $\sum_i x_i = 0$, $n^{-1}\sum_i x_i^2 = \frac{n^2 - 1}{3n^2} \ge \frac14$ and $n^{-1}\sum_i x_i^4 < 1$. Therefore the nested infimum of Theorem 2 at these constants lies in $[\max\{0, 1 - 1548/(n-1)\}, 1]$ and tends to $1 \ne 1 - \alpha$, for every $\alpha \in (0, 1)$. (d) [Exact finite illustration of (c), from the validator.] $n = 6$, $x_i = (2i - 7)/6$, all units compliers, $\beta = 7/3$, $y_i(0) = x_i$, $y_i(1) = \beta + 2x_i$, $n_1 = 3$: the model is in $\Xi_6(1, 0, 1/4, 4, 1/2, 1/4)$ with $\bar\beta = 7/3$ and heterogeneous effects; for each of the 20 assignments $\Delta_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta) = 0$ and $\beta \in I^{\mathrm{adj},*}_{1-\alpha}(Z)$, although 312 of the 400 values of $\Delta^{*2}_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)$ over pairs $(Z, Z^*)$ are non-zero.

canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: Part (a) (for every $n \ge 2$, the fourth-moment bound with constant $1/2$ forces a real vector to vanish; more generally, for a non-constant vector the ratio in Assumption 3(ii) is at least $\{(n-1)/n\}^{1/2}$) is an exact finite statement; the validator's artifact check.lean proves it in Lean 4 ('collapse_moments', 'moment_half_forces_zero') in the form $16(n-1)^2\sum_i v_i^4 \le n(\sum_i v_i^2)^2 \Rightarrow \sum_i v_i^2 = 0$.
